description.text: Carlo Pisacane was an Italian revolutionary who played a prominent role in the short‑lived Roman Republic of 1849, where he served as a military commander and chief of staff.  After the republic fell, he became best known for leading the ill‑fated Sapri uprising in 1857, an attempt to ignite a southern insurgency against the Bourbon monarchy.  The expedition ended in bloodshed at Sanza, where Pisacane chose suicide rather than surrender.

Beyond his military exploits, Pisacane evolved into a thinker who blended nationalist aspirations with early utopian socialist ideas.  He argued that true national liberation required a simultaneous social revolution that would free peasants from feudal landowners and establish a non‑hierarchical, cantonal society.  His writings and the example he set influenced later Italian anarchists and contributed to the spread of Bakuninist thought in the country.

curiosities.text: Pisacane is regarded as one of the first Italian proponents of utopian socialism, a stance that set him apart from contemporaries such as Giuseppe Mazzini.
